title: Guitar lessons, dancing school trio and Armand's Pass Christian band
summary: A grandmother, an aunt's ukulele and three failed classical guitar lessons come first. Ragtime players at a neighbour's dancing school then draw him back to the guitar. He takes cheap lessons from the chauffeur-bandleader Armand and hears Buddy Petit's band compete with him.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: My grandmother is actually the one who got me interested in music. She used to play piano a little bit and she'd get songs and knew enough about them. I remember probably the first two that she tried to teach me was one of them. Oh, my baby, my curly-headed baby, we'll sit beneath the sky and sing a song to the moon. That was one of them. And the other one was, I forget. But then I had an aunt that made a trip to Hawaii and brought back the first ukulele that I ever saw in my life. She brought it to me. And I fiddled with it a little bit. Regular four string like the modern one? Four string. Smaller to me. Smaller. Even as a child, when things usually look large, it looked smaller to me then. But they had a book of instructions and I couldn't get a thing out of it. Now, around, when I was around eight or nine, maybe ten even, my mother and father decided that I should take music and I picked the guitar. And they hired a very sweet lady who was the sister of a doctor, Miss Caznavet. She was very lovely and she really knew how to play a guitar. But classics, you know, Fandango and all that stuff. And she began with Solfegeo and all that business. Well, I lasted exactly three lessons and they told me that I was hopeless. Nothing pleased me more than twenty years later to be invited to a recital. Bernie Shields and I were the featured artists and she was on the front row. But then, Bill, the guitar got put aside. Yeah. And it just molded in the case. Until some people living two doors from us. There was our house, no, first my grandfather's, then my house, then the Stevens, and the next door was the Victor Greenmire family. And they decided to have dancing lessons. And I remember I had a damn good lambing because I wouldn't go. I had to get all dressed up and polished and I didn't want to go where there was girls anyhow. But when I got there, there was a little old dried up lady. She must have been seventy then and she lived to be ninety and still worked professionally playing ragtime on the piano. All we did was a two step then. And I remember. How old were you then? I must have been about eight and nine. At most ten. And then when the dancing school got going real good, they used to have three pieces. A piano, a guitar, and a bass. Real ragtime. And they switched from this white woman to three Negroes. Well, nobody beat me after that. I used to hang around the band and watch the guitar play. And that's when I began going home fooling around with it. Then the next move that made me get more deeply involved in it, I used to go across to past Christiane to visit the George W. Clays. And they were first at Bay St. Louis and then past Christiane. And I brought my guitar along with me and one of their boys played a mandolin and piano, younger than I was. And I discovered, they used to have bands play, oh maybe once a month for big dances over there. And I asked the guitar player if I could come to his place to get lessons. And he charged me twenty-five cents an hour. I had to walk about fifteen blocks both ways. It was a little shack way in the back. And the family was just up in arms that I was doing such a thing. But he'd get a mandolin and I'd get a guitar and he'd just sit me down and begin playing. Now that band was, I don't remember the name of his last name. The leader was their chauffeur. His name was Armand, A-R-M-A-N-D. Not P-R-R-O-N. But Armand was his first name. And they had a full eight or nine piece band which even back, well you add from age ten that would make it what about, Nineteen seven, nineteen seven, nineteen eight. They had two saxes in the band. And even that, yes sir, even that early. They were competing with Buddy Petit's band at the same time. Buddy Petit was as we know in Covington, Mandeville, Bita Springs in that area. But once in a while they'd bring him in to play and there would be a competition between these two bands. And that's why I heard Buddy Petit a great deal. I was amazed by his neck would swell out so far. Did anybody else tell you that about his playing?
